---
title: "Architecture"
guide-section: "Understanding replaylab"
---

# The one-paragraph version

replaylab decides **which designed proteins to test in a wet lab**. A pool of
designs has predicted metrics; an agent buys batches under a budget, results
come back (immediately or after a delay), and the agent decides what to buy
next and when to stop. Every strategy is validated offline by **replaying**
recorded real outcomes (Adaptyv's Proteinbase data); the same code is meant to
drive a live campaign later.

# Data flow

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    CSV["proteinbase.csv"] -->|build_tables| TABLES["designs / outcomes / targets<br/>(parquet)"]
    TABLES -->|build_clusters| CLUSTERS["clusters.csv"]
    TABLES -->|build_folds| FOLDS["folds.csv"]
    TABLES --> POOL["Pool<br/>visible features only"]
    TABLES --> HIDDEN["hidden outcomes"]
    POOL --> ENV["build_replay_campaign<br/>(aliases by seed)"]
    CLUSTERS --> ENV
    FOLDS --> ENV
    HIDDEN --> ENV
    ENV --> STATE["CampaignState<br/>snapshot"]
    STATE -->|policy.choose(state, k, rng)| IDS["batch of design ids"]
    IDS --> SUBMIT["Campaign.submit<br/>ticks the clock, stores events"]
    SUBMIT --> BACKEND["Backend.poll<br/>outcomes arrive"]
    BACKEND --> STATE
    SUBMIT --> SCORE["settle + score"]
    SCORE --> CARD["ScoreCard"]
```

# The layers

```{mermaid}
flowchart TB
    subgraph world["The world"]
        engine["engine<br/>the rules of the game"] --> store["store<br/>SQLite persistence"]
        engine --> backends["backends<br/>where outcomes come from"]
        engine --> datasets["datasets<br/>tables, clustering, the pool"]
        engine --> config["config<br/>YAML loading"]
        store --> domain["domain<br/>core types, stdlib only"]
        backends --> domain
        datasets --> domain
        datasets --> config
        config --> domain
    end
    subgraph agent["The agent"]
        policies["policies<br/>scripted strategies"] --> advisor["advisor<br/>pure functions over a snapshot"]
        advisor --> domain
        advisor --> datasets
        policies --> domain
    end
    eval["eval<br/>offline evaluation"] -.-> engine
    eval -.-> policies
The split is not cosmetic: `tests/test_import_boundaries.py` fails the build
if a package imports outside its lane.

::: {.callout-note}
**The rule that matters:** `advisor` and `policies` never import `store`,
`backends` or `engine`. They receive a
[`CampaignState`](../reference/domain.CampaignState.qmd) snapshot and nothing
else, so they *cannot* write and *cannot* see outcomes the campaign has not
bought. That is the architectural half of the leak protection; the rest is
below.
:::

# Persistence and kill-and-resume

The [`CampaignStore`](../reference/store.CampaignStore.qmd) (SQLite) records
every mutation as one transaction, and batches only ever move forward:
`proposed → submitted → partial → complete`. Alongside the tables there is an
**append-only event log**. `build_replay_campaign` replays that log to
reconstruct the replay backend's exact state, so a process that is killed mid
campaign picks up where it stopped and ends in *exactly* the same state as an
uninterrupted run (tested for delay 0 and delay 2).

# The leak rules

Hidden outcomes must never reach a strategy before it buys the design. Three
independent layers enforce this:

1. **Architecture** — the import boundaries above; policies only see snapshots.
2. **API shape** — the [`ReplayBackend`](../reference/backends.ReplayBackend.qmd)
   serves an outcome only via `submit` + `poll` after its delay; there is no
   bulk accessor to leak through.
3. **Guards** — `load_outcomes` refuses to read the held-out split outside the
   final run (`HeldOutAccessError`), and the ladder refuses held-out games with
   `ValueError`. Real ids never appear in state or in any file the store
   writes: agents see `d0001`-style aliases.

# Determinism

No global random state, no `hash()` of strings, no dependence on dict or set
ordering for output. Randomness comes only from a seeded
`numpy.random.Generator` that is passed in (`make_rng(seed, round)`), so the
same state and the same seed always produce the same batch — which is what
makes 100-seed ladder tables reproducible.
